title: Middle East watch
dek: One war, three fronts: Iran's sanctioned exports under the naval blockade, tanker movement through the Strait of Hormuz, and Houthi pressure on Red Sea shipping. The fronts move together; this page tracks them together. Every number is either tracker-observed or claimed, never both; bullets say which. When any front tightens, buyers bid up substitute sours and the whole complex firms, supporting Canadian differentials; when they loosen, medium and heavy sours soften.

claims.text: UKMTO said a vessel was struck by an unknown projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera, UAE, on Friday, with a fire later extinguished; maritime security sources identified it as the Panama-flagged crude supertanker GEM NO.2, fully laden at anchor, and said the strike outside the Hormuz area signaled widening tanker risk.

The US Treasury imposed fresh Iran sanctions on Oct 8 under 'Operation Economic Outcast,' designating 17 tankers plus individuals and networks moving Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals. Treasury officials said Iran has stopped loading and offloading crude and has only about 20 million barrels left on vessels outside the blockade.

Kpler data showed crude crossing the Strait of Hormuz fell 27% week over week to about 10.1 million b/d on Oct 8, with only seven commodity carriers transiting on Tuesday, the lowest since late July, as fresh Iranian tanker strikes and record Persian Gulf freight rates tightened vessel supply.

Saudi civil aviation authority GACA confirmed two Houthi strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Oct 8 that destroyed a parked Saudia aircraft and killed three people including a Saudia pilot; more than 150 flights were cancelled Thursday as Etihad, Qatar Airways, Flydubai, PIA, EgyptAir and Oman Air suspended services.

President Trump said Oct 8 the US would not attack Iran before the Nov 3 midterm elections amid 'productive discussions,' while Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran is reviewing the US response to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days; Brent fell about 1.3% Friday to roughly $103.

Since the war began in late February, 93 ships have been hit and 24 seafarers killed, Splash247 reported; the shrinking pool of willing crews is pushing tanker captain pay as high as $100,000 a month plus $50,000 per Hormuz transit, with war-risk insurance for single tanker voyages climbing to $20 million and some tanker earnings nearing $1.3 million a day.

Twelve seafarers were injured when the 114,600-dwt LR2 tanker On Peace was struck by a projectile while crossing the Strait of Hormuz; UKMTO confirmed the incident and the wounded were hospitalised in Khasab, Oman, on Oct 6.

Yemen's Houthis claimed three operations on Oct 6 using ballistic and cruise missiles plus drones, targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh, and military sites across southern Saudi Arabia, and warned international airlines against using Saudi airspace; Saudi authorities did not immediately comment.

Saudi naval forces struck military targets in the Houthi-held Red Sea port of Hodeidah, destroying weapons depots and facilities holding booby-trapped boats and naval mines, coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said, adding that the operation prevented a planned attack on shipping routes in the southern Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline was halted again on Oct 4 after a fresh attack damaged a pumping station at Khurais, east of Riyadh, a source in the kingdom's energy sector told Agence France-Presse. The source said the Khurais station had not been targeted before and the damage was extensive; Kpler data cited in the report shows the line's flows had already been halted from Sep 11 to Sep 22, and the pipeline has become essential to Saudi exports since the Hormuz blockade cut the main route.

UKMTO issued four warnings and an advisory on Oct 5 as attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz intensified, including a projectile strike that set a ship's engine room on fire with the crew still fighting it and no casualties reported. UKMTO also logged Iranian forces hailing the Liberia-registered tanker Singapore Energy 11 nm north of Oman with a warning it would be fired upon unless it turned back, plus time-late reports of Oct 3-4 strikes on an LPG tanker and two crude tankers, bringing its October count to nine reports.

A Bangladeshi national, Md Sajib Hossain of Cumilla, was killed on Oct 4 when a Houthi missile or drone struck a Saudi Aramco facility at Al Khurais, according to a Bangladesh foreign ministry press release issued Oct 5. The ministry condemned the attack and said its Riyadh embassy is coordinating with Saudi authorities to repatriate the body; it is the first independently reported casualty from the Oct 4 Houthi strikes on Aramco sites, which Saudi Arabia itself has still not commented on.

Oil prices rose on October 4 after the Houthis said they fired ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area, in retaliation for about 50 Saudi-led strikes in Yemen that Saudi Arabia has not confirmed. Brent crude futures rose 81 cents to $103.06 a barrel and US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) gained 46 cents to $91.57 a barrel.

Iran's Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad resigned for personal reasons and President Masoud Pezeshkian accepted the resignation, state media said on October 4. Hamid Bovard, chief executive of the government-owned National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC), was named acting minister. Paknejad had held the post since August 2024 and departs seven months into the US-Iran war, which has squeezed Iran's economy and oil exports.

The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported that Houthi forces captured the key supply route between the cities of Taiz and Aden on October 4, part of their campaign to seize Taiz City. Yemen's government announced an offensive across all fronts against the Houthis, but ISW's Critical Threats Project had not yet observed any offensive action. The loss of government-held ground narrows the protected corridor around the Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb approach.
claims.source: Institute for the Study of War

claims.text: Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi announced the start of a major military operation to retake Houthi-held territory, with Saudi Arabia leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground; the announcement followed weeks of preparations aimed at reversing the Houthis' seizure of the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

Treasury officials briefing after the Oct 8 designations said Iran has about 20 million barrels of crude left on vessels outside the blockade, off Singapore, Malaysia and China, that Tehran has stopped loading and offloading crude under the blockade, and that US forces boarded the sanctioned tanker Davina in the Indian Ocean; Trump said the US is having productive discussions with Iran and will not attack before the Nov 3 midterms.

Saudi Aramco unexpectedly cut its November crude prices for Asian buyers to six-year lows, Reuters reported, while OPEC+ delayed a review that would set members' 2027 output quotas after the Iran war disrupted capacity expansion projects across the Middle East. Two sources told Reuters the delay throws estimates of future production potential into uncertainty.

Iran's rial fell to a new record low on Saturday as the central bank announced an injection of up to $2 billion to support the currency, which has lost more than half its value over the past year under U.S. sanctions and the naval blockade. The free-market dollar traded around 2.688 million rials, up from 2.632 million on Friday, with state banks selling dollars under the central bank's directive.

The physical oil market is pricing a far tighter situation than futures: Europe's Dated Brent benchmark jumped above $120 per barrel even as ICE Brent sat near $101, a divergence the report ties to droned tankers in Hormuz, the European diesel release, and China's reinstated refined-product export ban.
Iran's seaborne oil exports were 587 million barrels in 2024 (+10.75% y/y); China took 533 million barrels, 91% of the total, up 24% from 2023.
Iran exported 666 million barrels in 2025 (+13.5% y/y), with China by far the largest buyer.

May 2026 exports by sea were just 2.01 million barrels vs 29.7 million in April (-93%); the May total was four Panamax/Handymax naphtha shipments to China plus limited liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). Very large crude carrier (VLCC) 2-million-barrel crude shipments dropped to zero.

Iran's pre-war baseline exports were 1.68 million b/d; TankerTrackers estimated they had fallen to zero by early September 2026 and could remain there 'for the foreseeable future' depending on any agreement.

Iran's export stream is medium and heavy sour crude: Iran Light (medium sour, American Petroleum Institute (API) gravity 33.6, 1.46% sulfur) and Iran Heavy (heavy sour, API gravity about 29.5, sulfur about 1.77%), per National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) assays reported by S&P Global Platts.
claims.source: Hellenic Shipping News (citing S&P Global Platts)

claims.text: China's independent refiners buy mainly Iran Light and some Iran Heavy. They crack Iran Light directly in their crude distillation units; Iran Heavy has to be blended with lighter grades first.

Iran Light is a direct substitute for Russian Urals in China's teapot refineries (independent refiners): similar medium sour specs (Iran Light 33.6 API and 1.46% sulfur vs Urals 31.7 API and 1.19%), and teapot sources say Iranian barrels suit their units better than Russian ones.

So the grades hit hardest by a return are medium and heavy sours: Russian Urals first (direct teapot substitute), then the wider medium-sour complex. Light sweets are less exposed, though record ESPO premiums of $20 to $30 per barrel over Brent would also ease.
UANI's 'ghost armada' reached 560 tracked tankers at end-2025 after 83 new vessels were identified during the year; of 180 tankers sanctioned in 2025, 108 had been previously identified by UANI.

China imported ~431 million barrels of Iranian oil in 2023 (over 80% of Iran's exports), rising to ~533 million in 2024 (over 91%), largely via ghost-fleet tankers offloading through intermediaries before reaching China.
claims.source: Claire Jungman, UANI (House Foreign Affairs testimony)

claims.text: Fox News reported that Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, which moves roughly 2.6 to 4 million b/d of crude from the Gulf to the Red Sea, could stay largely offline for three to five weeks of repairs after the Oct 4 attack damaged a pumping station at Khurais.

Kpler data reported by CNBC put the seven-day average of crude transiting Hormuz at 13.5 million b/d as of September 28, matching the firm's pre-war baseline for the corridor, while total Middle East Gulf crude shipments including Red Sea outlets ran about 16.5 million b/d in September excluding Iran. The recovery is not a return to normal: over 70 percent of crude crossing the strait changed tankers off Fujairah or Oman in August, refined-product flows through Hormuz remain only about 677,000 b/d versus roughly 3.6 million b/d before the war, and Iran's own crude loadings have effectively hit zero.

War-risk premiums for Saudi-linked tankers loading at Yanbu have risen to about 3% of vessel value from below 1% in early July, while ports further south face quotes as high as 7%, after the London marine insurance market classified the waters as high risk following Houthi attacks near the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

The New York Times reported that Iran is conducting roughly 30 drone attacks and 10 missile attacks per week on commercial vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz, a tempo that has turned the strait back into a direct tanker-safety corridor rather than just a congestion problem.

EIA estimated LNG flows through Hormuz fell to 0.8 billion cubic feet per day in the second quarter of 2026, from about 10.5 to 11.4 billion cubic feet per day before the conflict; the agency said its figures supplement vessel tracking with origin, destination and route analysis because AIS signals have become unreliable in the conflict zone.

EIA's quarterly Hormuz series shows the collapse in stages: 20.4 million b/d in Q1 2025, 21.6 million b/d in Q4 2025 before the war, 14.6 million b/d in Q1 2026 after the February 28 strikes, then 4.9 million b/d in Q2 2026. The Q1 2026 split was about 10.7 million b/d of crude and condensate plus 3.9 million b/d of products, down from 14.3 and 6.1 a year earlier.
claims.vintage: Data through Q2 2026; EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook reporting, Aug-Sep 2026

claims.text: EIA figures show Hormuz oil flows fell from 21.6 million b/d in Q4 2025 to just 4.9 million b/d in Q2 2026, while Bab el-Mandeb flows rose from 5.4 to 8.1 million b/d, a major rerouting of the global oil transportation system.

IEA's September 2026 Oil Market Report said more than 10 million b/d of Gulf output remained shut in amid security risks; cumulative supply losses since February exceeded 507 million barrels of observed inventory draws.
claims.vintage: Data through Aug 2026; report Sep 11, 2026; accessed 2026-09-23
claims.source: Namibia Daily News (via Xinhua, citing IEA September OMR)

claims.text: The Baltic VLCC time-charter average rose from ~$198,000/day in July to ~$449,000/day in the first half of September, reaching ~$722,946/day by September 18, 2026, versus ~$79,700/day in mid-September 2025.

Iran's IRGC Navy claimed it struck the LPG carrier NV Sunshine south of the Strait of Hormuz for using an 'illegal route,' saying the engine room caught fire; the vessel's owner told AAP the tanker was not attacked, is operating normally, and all crew are safe.

The Houthis hit Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport with two cruise missiles on Thursday, killing three Saudi nationals and injuring several; Europe's EASA widened its Saudi airspace advisory on Friday, OPSGROUP advised members to avoid Saudi Arabia, and airlines including Lufthansa, Etihad and flydubai cancelled Riyadh flights, with 131 cancellations by Friday afternoon per Flightradar24.

Attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest weekly level since the Iran war began on February 28, with at least 12 attacks on oil, LNG and LPG tankers in the week of September 28 to October 5, according to three maritime security sources; the UN's International Maritime Organization logged nine incidents for the same week.

UKMTO reported that a tanker was struck by multiple projectiles 51 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar, with casualties reported and authorities investigating; it is the first reported attack that deep inside the Persian Gulf since a tanker was hit southeast of Al-Faw, Iraq, on September 9.

Yemen's Houthis attacked Aden's international airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones early Wednesday, Yemen's Transport Ministry said; the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a separate Houthi ballistic missile launched toward the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait.

Three people were killed and 36 wounded in attacks on two Saudi airports, the kingdom's civil aviation authorities said: one killed and eight wounded at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, and two killed and 28 wounded at Abha airport. The Saudi-led coalition vowed retaliation and said it had attacked more than 80 Houthi military sites across Saada, Hodeidah, Jawf and Marib.

IRGC commander-in-chief's adviser Mohammadreza Naqdi told Fars News Agency that the Strait of Hormuz is closed and under full control of Iran's armed forces until Iran's demands are met, and said Iran will soon block the remaining routes hugging Oman's coast; US Central Command on Oct 7 publicly rejected the claim as false, saying traffic was flowing with about 20 million barrels of crude moving through. Provisional Kpler data put regional crude exports at a seven-day moving average of 18.3 million b/d on September 30, topping pre-war levels on 14 days in September.

UKMTO logged five incidents on Oct 5 in and near the Strait of Hormuz: four tanker attacks, including delayed reports of an Oct 4 strike on an inbound LPG tanker and another on a crude oil tanker, plus an inbound tanker hailed by IRGC forces off Khasab, Oman, and ordered to turn back or risk being targeted; the tanker complied.

President Trump said on Oct 6 he was 'always open' to direct talks with Iran, even as UKMTO logged a ninth ship attack in the region within a week; the remarks followed a reported Camp David meeting where Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Rubio discussed next steps in the Iran war.

Iran's parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said on Oct 4 that the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions from a June interim agreement with the US are met, adding that Washington must understand the period of dragging out the process and dictating one-sided demands is over. The statement followed Tehran's receipt, via Qatari mediators, of the US reply to its UN General Assembly proposal for a seven-day reopening; the Foreign Ministry stressed its current focus is Hormuz security, not nuclear talks, and denied offering IAEA inspections for sanctions relief.

Fighting centered on Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, with the Houthis reporting 55 of their fighters killed on Oct 2 while government sources told AFP 26 troops had died; Saudi authorities separately reported a Houthi projectile damaged a school in the border city of Najran.

The US Treasury designated the Kremlin-linked A7 financial network a 'significant transnational criminal organization,' saying its subagents disguised payments involving sanctioned entities as legitimate commercial transactions to help Russian and Iranian entities move money outside the banking system, including for Iranian oil sales and weapons procurement. FinCEN said A7 subagents processed more than $17 billion between January 2025 and June 2026. A7 denied any Iran links on October 2.

The U.S. is sending roughly 9,000 troops aboard ships to the Middle East, including the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island amphibious group, potentially putting three carrier groups in the region. President Trump told Time it is possible he ramps up bombing of Iran after the Nov 3 elections, and said Iran offered to open the Strait of Hormuz in its latest ceasefire proposal, which he rejected as not good enough.

Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia is planning an offensive to push the Houthis off the Bab el-Mandeb strait, citing six Gulf and Yemeni officials and Western diplomats; Riyadh is weighing either a focused coastal assault or a broader multi-front campaign in Al-Bayda, Marib, Taiz and Al-Jawf that could mobilize more than 100,000 Yemeni troops, with timing estimates ranging from within a week to after the US midterm elections.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said a crude tanker was struck by an unknown projectile on October 3 about four nautical miles east of Oman, and a second tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz on October 4 with damage to its engine room. Crews were reported safe and no environmental damage was recorded. Separately, Iran's parliament speaker said the strait will not fully reopen until seven conditions under the Islamabad Memorandum are met.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group struck an Aramco oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones late on Oct 3, sparking fires, and an AFP journalist reported seeing firefighters battling a blaze at Aramco's Riyadh refinery south of the capital; the Houthis also said Saudi Arabia launched 94 strikes on Houthi-held areas in the preceding 24 hours.

G7 leaders agreed Oct 2 to release up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves over four months via the IEA, starting immediately, with substantial diesel in the first 20 days and further diesel releases under discussion. The joint statement also called for restoring navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

Five Indian nationals aboard the struck Kuwait-flagged VLCC Kazimah III were brought ashore in Oman after the Embassy of India in Oman coordinated the rescue, with Omani authorities assisting. India says more than 4,500 Indian seafarers are currently on commercial vessels in the region.

Iranian outlets reported a supertanker able to carry 2.5 million barrels was hit about 8 kilometers off the Omani coast while sailing what Iran's Fars News Agency called an 'unauthorized route' south of the strait, and caught fire. UKMTO confirmed it had received a report of a tanker incident; the vessel's identity and the Fars account were not independently corroborated.

Three tankers were hit by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on September 29, according to time-late reports received by UKMTO: the Liberia-flagged, AIS-dark VLCC Mersin Prosperity, the Aframax Sinbad and the products tanker Al Ruwais, identified by shipping intelligence firm Marisks (carried by Reuters). A separate September 28 strike on a tanker caused a fire that has since been extinguished, with the vessel underway and crew safe.

Bab el-Mandeb traffic fell to 11 commodity-vessel transits on September 27, the lowest in months, after Houthi strikes on Saudi coastal installations; on September 25 the Houthis captured Mayun island at the Red Sea entrance, a key position over the alternative lane for Saudi oil while Hormuz is disrupted.

Diplomacy stalled: President Trump rejected Iran's seven-day Hormuz reopening proposal on September 26, and the Wall Street Journal reported US officials expect airstrikes to resume after the November midterms.
claims.source: Seoul Economic Daily (citing AFP/Reuters); Wall Street Journal

claims.text: The recovery split widened: Kpler's September snapshot put regional exports at 12.8 million b/d (highest since February), Hormuz at ~7.4 million b/d and Saudi Arabia at ~5.4 million b/d versus 2.4 million in August, while Iranian crude exports stayed at zero for 60+ days.

The Kuwait Oil Tanker Co VLCC Al Funtas, struck by a suspected projectile north of Khasab on September 28, had its onboard fire extinguished, all crew safe and no environmental impact reported, with the vessel remaining underway toward a port of refuge rather than becoming disabled inside the chokepoint.

UKMTO said three tankers were struck by unknown projectiles in separate attacks on September 29: one crude carrier struck on the port side, one tanker transiting inbound, and one LNG carrier, bringing the total to four vessels hit since the Al Funtas VLCC was struck, according to verified sources cited by TradeWinds and corroborated by UKMTO-sourced reports.

TradeWinds, citing UK maritime security firm Ambrey, reported that Iran struck a VLCC in the strait in the early hours of September 29, setting off a fire aboard with no fatalities; Ambrey believes the vessel is the 317,000-dwt Al Funtas (built 2017), owned by Kuwait Oil Tanker Co, though TradeWinds noted no other Iranian or Western source had confirmed the strike at the time of writing. Lloyd's List also reported a Kuwait Oil Tanker Co vessel struck in the strait on September 29, citing Kingdom Exploration.
claims.source: TradeWinds (citing Ambrey); Lloyd's List (via Kingdom Exploration)

claims.text: Kpler data showed crude and refined-product volumes through Hormuz averaged about 13.1 million b/d last week, close to 80% of the roughly 17.1 million b/d that traversed the chokepoint before the war, driven by US Navy-backed shuttles, ship-to-ship transfers, and dark transits, with Kpler's Matt Smith calling Iran's grip on the strait increasingly tenuous.

Saudi Arabia restarted tanker loadings at Yanbu after repairing its East-West Pipeline, restoring the Hormuz-bypass outlet; Kpler put current pipeline throughput at about 2.65 million b/d rising toward 3 to 4 million b/d, though a return to the pre-attack rate near 5.5 million b/d could take another month.

Iranian state media claimed August 2026 oil exports above $3 billion, the highest monthly figure in two years, sharply at odds with tracker estimates of ~220-255 kb/d loaded that month; treat as claimed, not tracked.

For the first time in two months, aggregate crude exports out of the US blockade line by Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE and Oman averaged north of 10 million b/d; Iranian crude exports remained at zero, with 'not a single barrel of crude oil' coming out of Iran over the past 60 days.

Middle East crude exports were down 39% in August versus a January-February baseline of 18.5 million b/d; the shortfall from that baseline narrowed to 7.2 million b/d, from a peak deficit of 12.4 million in May when exports were down 67%.

Vortexa's own write-up (Sep 15) put Iranian crude loadings at around 210 kb/d in August, the lowest since 2020 and down from roughly 2 million b/d earlier in 2026, and said the barrels still loading are not translating into fresh Iranian crude clearing the Gulf. The 210 kb/d (Vortexa, crude-only) and the 220,000-255,000 b/d (Reuters aggregation of Kpler, Vortexa and TankerTrackers, crude plus condensate) describe the same August; the gap is condensate, not a disagreement.
Iranian floating crude was ~29 million barrels on September 8, 2026, down from ~90 million in mid-July, the blockade drew down pre-war floating stock by roughly two-thirds (Kpler, via WSJ).
claims.source: WSJ via Kpler (compiled in Oil Depletion Report)

claims.text: Iran sold about 9 million barrels (~$900M) out of floating storage in the Gulf of Oman, vessels already clear of Iranian ports when enforcement began, hence outside the blockade's reach.

An estimated 40-50 million barrels of Iranian oil remained on the water in Asia, with Chinese discharges running near 1 million b/d; Tehran selling from already-cleared floating storage it cannot replenish.
27 sanctioned tankers were waiting off Sri Lanka in ballast, part of the shadow fleet left idle by the blockade.

Scarcity is already pricing in: Kpler reported Iran Light flipping from a $3.50 per barrel discount to a $3.50 premium over Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) Brent within a week as available floating cargoes thinned.

Kpler put total Iranian crude outside the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman at about 83 million barrels, with about 40 million at Singapore's Eastern Outer Port Limits (EOPL) anchorage, but only about 4 million barrels of that still unsold. An unwind would mostly deliver already-sold cargoes, not flood the spot market.

The reroute path back is Kharg Island loadings, transit through the Gulf of Oman, ship-to-ship transfer at EOPL Malaysia, delivery to Shandong teapots. Kpler notes teapots have been substituting Russian Urals and fuel oil while Iranian barrels were blocked, with the Eastern Siberia-Pacific Ocean (ESPO) blend sold out weeks in advance.

Six tankers carrying an estimated 10.5 million barrels of Iranian oil were forced back to Iran in recent days under the US blockade, per ship-tracking data and satellite analysis; Kpler and SynMax counted only seven vessels transiting Hormuz in the previous 24 hours, none carrying oil for the global market.

No fresh sanctions designations on shadow-fleet vessels or entities appeared from the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control, the European Union, the United Kingdom, or the United Nations in the past week, per sanctions tracker Eagle Intelligence, leaving the enforcement picture flat even as Hormuz tensions raised tanker insurance costs.

Tracking data showed the tankers Tifani and Majestic X, seized by US forces in April, sailing along Brazil's northern coast while the June-seized Lenore rounded the Cape of Good Hope into the Atlantic, carrying nearly 6 million barrels of Iranian crude worth about $600 million toward the United States for expected forfeiture.

TankerTrackers identified two US-sanctioned tankers in ballast that penetrated the blockade inbound for Iran with Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders on; the US Navy claims 13 Iranian tankers have been turned back so far.

Kpler data showed 33.7 million barrels of crude shipped out via Hormuz in the week starting September 20, through 19 tankers including 17 VLCCs, roughly on track with the prior week; a US official told Reuters that on September 24 about 60 commercial vessels transited the strait carrying the highest daily crude volume since early July.

Reuters, citing Kpler, reported that Middle East crude exports rebounded in September to 16.328 million b/d, the highest since the war started; Hormuz exports were set to hit about 9.719 million b/d, with Saudi Arabia on track to ship about 5.4 million b/d versus 2.446 million b/d in August, though still about 3.2 million b/d below February's 19.513 million b/d; Kpler put regional exports at just under 80% of pre-conflict levels.

Kpler tracked nine Hormuz commodity-vessel transits on September 24, down from 14 the day before and below the 10-day average of about 18; Kpler estimated 33.7 million barrels of crude exported in the week beginning September 20, with 17 of the 19 crude tankers tracked that week being very large crude carriers, which is why barrel flows can run ahead of vessel counts.

Kpler data showed September crude transits through Hormuz rebounding to 10.1 million b/d month-to-date, up nearly 70.5 percent from the full month of August and the first time above 10 million b/d since the war began; Kpler's Matt Smith called it a solid rebound, while noting February moved just over 16 million b/d of crude in the war's first days.

The Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was hit by an unknown projectile on September 23, caught fire and went adrift, with UKMTO reporting one Indian seafarer killed and one injured; preliminary Kpler data cited by Reuters showed only two commodity vessels crossed the strait on September 21, against about 125 large commercial vessels per day before the war.
claims.source: SAFETY4SEA (citing UKMTO; Kpler data via Reuters)

claims.text: US Central Command said it had redirected 122 commercial vessels as of September 25, up from 115 on September 23 and 110 on September 21.

Vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz held at 12 crossings on September 23, unchanged from September 22: about 10 vessels inbound and two outbound, per Windward data. Three inbound vessels used the southern US-assisted route and six took Iran's northern corridor; both outbound vessels used the southern route.

Recent tracking shows commodity-carrying Hormuz transits averaging roughly 10 vessels per day versus a pre-war baseline of around 85 - 90; throughput has been reported as low as ~7% of normal in some periods.

The White House signed H.R. 5334, the Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, into law September 18, 2026, expanding sanctions and tariff authority relating to Russia and Iran and the shadow tanker system supporting Russian energy exports.

TankerTrackers' Sep 14-15 satellite imagery analysis said the strait 'now hosts bi-directional daytime traffic of VLCC supertankers' and that 'greater volumes of crude oil, LNG and LPG are being exchanged via STS transfer in the Gulf of Oman' (no vessel count given). The same day it reported Saudi Arabia had loaded 8.7 million barrels at its east-coast terminals that day (a loading figure, not a Hormuz transit figure).

On Gulf ship-to-ship volumes the trackers are directionally aligned but measure different universes: Vortexa's published Sep 21 note put crude-on-VLCC STS from ports west of Hormuz at around 6 million b/d since end-August (about three VLCC pairs starting STS daily), with operations stretching to nearly 10 days from 5-7 and queues worsening; outlets quoting TankerTrackers put all-transfer STS at about 7.15 million b/d over the 14 days to mid-September, up 56% month-on-month (secondhand; treat as an estimate until the direct post is captured); Kpler's narrower Gulf-of-Oman STS read was about 2.5 million b/d for September versus 1.4 million in August. Editorial: Vortexa's is the firmest published figure; all three agree STS has surged to multi-million-b/d scale.

The 5-million-b/d East-West Petroline to Yanbu was knocked offline by drone strikes (one account dates them to Sep 10, another to Sep 13), and Yanbu loading halted from Sep 11. Aramco pivoted to eastern sea lanes, offering about 60 million barrels of Ras Tanura crude for Sep-Oct delivery via a two-tier shuttle: smaller tankers to Sohar, Oman, then ship-to-ship transfers onto deep-draft vessels for Asia. US CENTCOM said its forces had assisted about 2,000 commercial transits and moved over 1 billion barrels of Gulf oil over the prior couple of months.

Kpler's Homayoun Falakshahi (~Sep 12): 'It's exactly the opposite scenario compared to the beginning of the war where Iran could export its oil but the neighbors couldn't... And now it's actually the contrary. Iran cannot export new oil.' Hormuz crude-and-condensate flows recovered to around two-thirds of pre-war volumes (Goldman Sachs), roughly 70% on Kpler's broader read; the UAE contrast: shipments back within 0.02% of pre-war, running 3.7-4.3 million b/d June through September versus a March crater of about 1.9-2.13 million b/d.

On the Saudi September rebound the trackers agree: Kpler's September snapshot put Saudi exports at about 5.4 million b/d; Bloomberg ship-tracking had 5.28 million b/d for Sep 1-23. The Sep 21 east-coast surge reads 12-14 million barrels in 24 hours at Ras Tanura and Juaymah (Kpler counted six VLCCs, TankerTrackers seven supertankers), the largest single-day Gulf loading surge since the escalation; Saudi exports ran past 4 million b/d in mid-September from August's 2.4 million trough.
claims.source: Kpler; Bloomberg ship-tracking; TankerTrackers (via UAE Vartha)

claims.text: Kpler's September Hormuz figures look scattered until sorted by definition: about 7 million b/d of crude for the full week before Sep 20 (49.2 million barrels), 10.1 million b/d crude month-to-date, and above 13.5 million b/d all-liquids on a 7-day average (Sep 26). Same tracker, different windows and product universes; read the window before comparing.
Asia's Middle East imports ran 12.56 million b/d in September, still 3.53 million b/d below the pre-conflict average.
Oil prices rose above $102 a barrel as the Hormuz strikes intensified against vessels described as violating the strait's navigation rules.

Brent futures stayed above $103 a barrel on September 30 while WTI slipped to $89.24, with Brent set for roughly a 14% monthly advance, its best monthly performance since July, even as the physical market adjusted to rebounding Hormuz flows.
TradeWinds reported Brent crude hit $107 a barrel on September 29 as the reported Al Funtas strike landed, with tanker freight rates still at exorbitant levels.

Brent settled at $104.32 a barrel on September 25, down 2.1 percent, with WTI at $92.41, down 2.3 percent, as Iran's seven-day Hormuz proposal landed and the market priced a possible short-term thaw in Gulf shipping.

VLCC rates on West Asia - China routes hit a record $1.2 million a day, more than doubling since late August; Energy Aspects' Amrita Sen warned surging shipping costs could push delivered crude in Asia toward $150 a barrel.

War-risk insurance premiums were revised from peacetime levels of 0.5 - 1% of hull and machinery value to approximately 10%, millions of dollars in added cost per VLCC voyage, passed through to charterers.
US Gulf - China VLCC rates were reported at $400,000 per day and Middle East Gulf spot rates at $1.25 million per day in late September 2026.

IEA projects 2026 world oil supply averaging 100.7 million b/d, down 5.7 million b/d year-on-year, with full recovery of Middle East supplies deferred until 2027; global oil demand is forecast to fall 2.5 million b/d in 2026.

Kpler estimated Middle East Gulf crude exports reached about 16.5 million b/d in September, with about 40% leaving without crossing Hormuz compared with 17% before the war as Saudi Arabia and the UAE leaned on pipeline routes, and more than 70% of volumes changing tankers offshore: 'The volumes have recovered but through a fundamentally different export system.'

Saudi Aramco notified customers on September 28 of its October crude-loading schedule from Yanbu, Reuters reported, with trade sources putting loadings near 2 million barrels per day and Kpler estimating flows could reach 3 to 4 million barrels per day within days before a full recovery to the pre-attack rate of about 5.5 million barrels per day in roughly a month; Brent fell 2.6% on September 29 as traders focused on the export recovery.

Crude has started flowing again to Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports after repairs to the East-West Pipeline damaged by the September 10 drone attack, with the twin pipeline at about half of its 7 million b/d capacity according to Bloomberg sources; TankerTrackers identified about 40 tankers near Yanbu and Al Muajjiz with nearly 10 million barrels loading, while Kpler put Yanbu exports at 1.6 million b/d on a seven-day average versus 4 million b/d from April to July, and Ras Tanura loadings at 40 million barrels in September, the highest since the war began.

Brent rose more than 3 percent on September 24, briefly topping $108 a barrel, before easing to $105.77 on September 25 morning, as Houthi strikes on Yanbu added pressure on Saudi Arabia's oil exports; analysts said crude would likely stay above $100 a barrel as long as the war on Iran continued.

With Yanbu loadings suspended, Saudi Aramco cancelled or delayed some September crude cargoes to European refiners, which may need to source alternative barrels from the Americas, the North Sea, and Africa at higher freight costs; Kpler estimates cited at the time put Yanbu inventories below 15 million barrels, enough for only about four days of exports at 3.5 million barrels per day.

The Suez Canal Authority (SCA) reported that 5,874 vessels carrying 247.2 million tons transited the canal from July through mid-September 2026, generating $1.97 billion in revenue, up 5.2% in vessel count, 14.4% in tonnage, and 17.5% in revenue versus the same period last year; chairman Ossama Rabiee also projected canal revenue reaching about $8 billion in fiscal year 2026/27.
claims.source: State Information Service Egypt (quoting the Suez Canal Authority)

claims.text: COSCO Shipping Lines made its first southbound Suez transit since the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb tensions disrupted patterns, with the 24,188 twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU) OOCL Portugal sailing from Belgium to China on September 16; the Suez Canal Authority (SCA) said container-ship net tonnage through the canal reached about 72.1 million tonnes in January-August 2026, up 54.2% year on year, and that services by CMA CGM, Maersk, Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC), Hapag-Lloyd, and COSCO have returned to the canal on Europe-Asia trades.
claims.source: Container News (citing the Suez Canal Authority)

claims.text: War-risk pricing has split into tiers rather than one Red Sea number: indicative premiums for the southern Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb rose above 1% of vessel value from about 0.3% a week earlier, Saudi-linked voyages were quoted as high as 3%, while the northern Saudi Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Yanbu were quoted around 0.1%, a markedly different near-term risk profile.

Xeneta analyst Peter Sand said ocean freight is unlikely to return to Suez at scale for the rest of 2026, warning that renewed Houthi attacks would shelve any phased return; he estimates the Cape of Good Hope routing absorbs about 2.5 million TEU of the global 34 million TEU boxship fleet, shrinking available capacity by roughly 7%. Separately, leading protection and indemnity (P&I) clubs and their reinsurers are pulling war-risk cover for much of the Gulf region, effectively putting the Arabian Gulf off-limits for insurance purposes.

President Trump said on September 29 the US Navy would begin escorting tankers through Hormuz 'as soon as possible' and that he had ordered the US Development Finance Corporation to provide political risk insurance and guarantees for maritime trade, less than 24 hours after Navy officials told industry representatives there was 'no chance' of escorts.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented a seven-day proposal at the United Nations General Assembly on September 25, transmitted to Washington through Qatar: Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz to normal maritime passage and resume nuclear talks within seven days if the United States ends the naval blockade, waives sanctions on Iranian oil, releases at least $12 billion in frozen assets, and holds a ceasefire on all fronts, including Lebanon and Yemen.
claims.source: The Hindu BusinessLine (citing the Associated Press)

claims.text: Two tankers were attacked on the Omani side of the Strait of Hormuz, four nautical miles off Khasab on the Musandam Peninsula: about four projectiles hit the two vessels at roughly 1910 UTC, one caught fire and the other's status was unknown, according to a report UKMTO received from a nearby vessel's master. Iran has not claimed responsibility.
The current war was triggered February 28, 2026 by joint US and Israeli strikes on Iran; Iran responded by closing commercial access to Hormuz through vessel attacks and sea mining.

As of September 20, 2026, US Central Command said its forces had redirected 109 commercial vessels to enforce compliance with the US maritime blockade on traffic to and from Iranian ports, a blockade resumed July 14, 2026.

Between September 16 and 18, 2026, three tankers were struck in the strait; the Togo-flagged product tanker Trend was hit September 16 near Khasab and caught fire before the crew extinguished it. Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed the Trend attack, saying it was an illegal transit attempt, and warned any unauthorized passage would face 'destruction'.
A UKMTO security warning dated September 17, 2026 covered an attack 16 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman; the targeted vessel's crew were confirmed safe with no environmental impact.
UKMTO issued an advisory after the September 21 strike urging vessels operating in the area to transit with caution and report suspicious activity to authorities.

The Houthis said they struck two Saudi oil tankers, the Encelia and the Layla, with missiles and drones as part of a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia; Saudi state news agency SPA confirmed the Encelia was struck with a fire on its bow and all crew safe, while the Layla strike was unconfirmed; UKMTO reported an 'unknown projectile' striking a tanker about 130 km from Al Shuqaiq. The claim followed the group's announced maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia after a drone strike on the East-West Pipeline and an attempted attack on the Red Sea port of Yanbu.

Saudi authorities ordered Riyadh schools to switch to remote learning for a week after Saudi air defenses said they intercepted Houthi drones aimed at the capital and ballistic missiles targeting Khamis Mushait; a Houthi political bureau member described the raid as a small-scale rehearsal for a full escalation.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group struck Aramco sites in Jizan and Yanbu on September 26, a claim Riyadh did not confirm; Kpler data showed only 11 commodity vessels transited Bab el-Mandeb on September 27, the lowest in months, though two very large crude carriers were still sailing to Yanbu to load Saudi crude.

Yemen's Houthi rebels captured the island of Mayun at the entrance of the Red Sea on September 25, a key position over the alternative shipping lane for Saudi oil while Hormuz is disrupted; Saudi Arabia responded with airstrikes against the airport in Mokha, the Red Sea port the Houthis seized the day before.

The Houthis claimed missile and drone attacks on September 24 against Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu and a sensitive target in Riyadh; Saudi forces said they intercepted six ballistic missiles, with no damage confirmed by authorities.

The US Maritime Administration, in guidance effective September 23, urged US-flagged commercial vessels to switch off their Automatic Identification System (AIS) when transiting the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, and to vary routes and speeds and limit electronic transmissions, as Houthi attacks persist. Vessels with links to Israel, the US, the UK or Saudi Arabia are considered at greater risk.

Saudi Arabia restarted its East-West Pipeline (Petroline) on September 22, 2026 after a nine-day shutdown triggered by drone attacks on September 13, with the line pumping at a low rate and Saudi Aramco seeking to return toward about 4 million barrels per day, roughly 4% of global oil supply; one crude cargo was scheduled to load at Yanbu later that Tuesday bound for China, and the restart pressured Brent crude futures down more than $2 a barrel to their lowest since September 8.

Before the attack, the East-West Pipeline carried roughly 5.5 million barrels per day, of which about 4.5 million barrels per day of crude was exported through Yanbu to Mediterranean and northwest European refiners without routing through the Strait of Hormuz or Bab el-Mandeb; Houthi forces struck multiple pumping stations across two regions of Saudi Arabia on September 10, no crude has loaded from Yanbu since September 11, and terminal inventories were estimated to cover only three to five days of loadings at normal rates.

The Houthis claimed on September 23 that they struck the Saudi oil tanker Wafa with ballistic missiles off the coast of Yanbu, calling the strike precise but giving no details of damage or casualties; the claim was not independently verified and Saudi authorities did not immediately respond. The Houthi spokesperson also claimed eight Saudi oil tankers have been targeted since the campaign began with 29 others forced to turn back, figures that are self-reported.

Traffic through Bab el-Mandeb stayed volatile but open: 22 commodity vessels crossed on Tuesday, September 22 (14 toward the Red Sea, 8 toward the Gulf of Aden), below the 10-day average of about 26 but well above the single-digit levels seen through the Strait of Hormuz over the same weekend.

U.S. aviation sanctions have cut international movements at Tehran's Imam Khomeini airport by about 42 percent, far short of the 80 to 90 percent shutdown claimed by U.S. officials: FlightRadar24 data summarized by AFP show an average of 53 international movements a day since September 23 versus 91 before the compliance deadline. Flights to China held steady at about eight a day and Turkey service fell only 19 percent, while regular service to Georgia, Oman, Azerbaijan and Dubai stopped or was sharply reduced, and Iraq access remains contested.

As part of the market-management response, Bank Saderat began selling foreign currency at 60 selected branches on Saturday, with adults allowed up to $10,000 a year. The Iranian Foreign Ministry separately condemned U.S. aviation sanctions as illegal and urged Iraq to lift flight restrictions between the two countries.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on X that 'Iran loaded ZERO crude oil onto tankers in September,' describing the Trump administration's Operation Economic Outcast campaign as cutting off Tehran's most critical source of revenue.

The US Treasury sanctioned Iran's automotive and rail sectors under Operation Economic Outcast, designating Iran Khodro (IKCO) and SAIPA, which Treasury says make up more than 90% of the domestic auto market, plus the state-owned Islamic Republic of Iran Railway Company, Raja Passenger Trains and the Railway Transportation Company, and foreign suppliers in Indonesia, the UAE and Turkey. Treasury said the naval blockade has forced Tehran to lean on rail and road to move petroleum, fertilizer and chemicals, and the sanctions target those alternatives.

President Trump wrote on Truth Social on September 28 that he had offered Iran "NOTHING," denying Axios and CNN reports that a US official had said he was open to easing sanctions and releasing frozen funds in exchange for "concrete progress" on the nuclear file; President Pezeshkian told CBS the same day that Tehran was ready for talks but would not accept bullying or coercion.

Iran's state media said on September 28 that its UN General Assembly delegation had no meetings scheduled with the United States and would return to Tehran on Tuesday, after conveying its seven-condition demand list via a Qatari mediator.
claims.source: Dim Sum Daily (citing Iranian state media)

claims.text: The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump privately told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterm elections, when high gasoline prices would be less of a political consideration; the report accompanied a new estimate that the US naval blockade has doubled crude volumes exiting the Persian Gulf.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Fox News that about 15 million barrels remained in Iran's final oil shipments to China and that 'probably within two weeks, Iran will have very little left to trade,' describing the economic isolation campaign as 'Operation Economic Outcast.'
claims.source: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (via Fox News; Economy.ac)

claims.text: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on September 27 that Tehran's conditions remain unchanged and that only a negotiated solution can end the standoff, adding that mediators had not yet formally conveyed a US rejection; a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran will show no flexibility on uranium enrichment.

President Trump said on September 26 that he had rejected the seven-day proposal, which had conditioned reopening Hormuz on a region-wide ceasefire, release of about $12 billion in frozen assets, a waiver of oil sanctions and an end to the US naval blockade; the Wall Street Journal reported US officials expect airstrikes to resume after the November midterms.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters on September 25 that Iran would show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the United States accepts the Hormuz proposal, and that the waterway would stay closed until all of Iran's conditions are met. Tehran would give no concessions on enriching uranium or shipping highly enriched uranium out of the country, one of the main US demands. President Pezeshkian said he hopes for a deal before the November 3 midterm elections.

The US blockade of Iranian ports started April 13, 2026; United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI) measures exports by vessels crossing the blockade line from the eastern point of Oman to the Iran-Pakistan border, exiting the Gulf of Oman, rather than by point of loading.
Washington restored the blockade on July 14, 2026; Kpler, Vortexa and TankerTrackers identified no Iranian crude cargo vessel successfully transiting Hormuz to China after that date.
claims.source: National Security Journal (citing Vortexa, Kpler, Reuters)

claims.text: EIA estimated oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz averaged 20.9 million b/d in the first half of 2025, roughly 15 million b/d of crude oil and condensate plus about 5.5 million b/d of refined petroleum products.
IEA estimated about 20 million b/d of crude and products moved through Hormuz in 2025, roughly 25% of global seaborne oil trade and about 20% of world petroleum liquids consumption.
Of the Hormuz total, nearly 15 million b/d was crude oil, about 34% of all global crude oil trade in 2025; roughly 80% of the oil was destined for Asian markets.
Destination split of Hormuz crude in 2025: China ~25%, India ~19%, Japan ~13%, South Korea ~11%, other Asia ~17%, Europe ~9%, US ~3%; China and India together took 44% of flows.
Saudi Arabia is the dominant single-country contributor to Hormuz crude flows, about 38% or roughly 5.5 million b/d; Iraq, Kuwait, the UAE, Qatar and Iran make up the rest.
EIA estimated one-fifth of global LNG trade moved through Hormuz in 2024, primarily Qatari cargoes, IEA's February 2026 factsheet put it at almost 20% of global LNG exports.
claims.source: EIA Today in Energy (via GitHub essay)

claims.text: US crude and condensate imports through Hormuz were about 7% of total US crude and condensate imports in 2024 and about 2% of US petroleum liquids consumption.
claims.source: EIA Today in Energy (via GitHub essay)

claims.text: Saudi Arabia and the UAE have pipelines capable of bypassing the strait, but together they could provide only about 4.7 million b/d of bypass capacity, a fraction of normal ~21 million b/d traffic.
claims.vintage: Data: EIA estimate current through 2026; accessed 2026-09-23

claims.text: Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline carries crude from the kingdom's eastern producing region to Yanbu on the Red Sea, allowing Saudi oil to reach water without passing through Hormuz; it has become the main bypass artery during the current conflict.

Weekly transit volume through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait grew from 1.1 million to 1.5 million metric tons (roughly 32 to 38 vessel transits) between January and July 2026 as Hormuz disruption pushed traffic south, but contracted to 25 weekly transits carrying about 750,000 metric tons after Houthi missile strikes resumed in July; for scale, pre-October 2023 traffic averaged about 80 vessels and 3.4 million metric tons per week, so Red Sea shipping is still below a third of its old normal.
claims.vintage: Data: Jan-Jul 2026 and pre-2023 baseline; accessed 2026-09-24

claims.text: Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif said on September 29 that Islamabad would use 'whatever means are available' to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, while declining to say whether Pakistani forces had already taken part in strikes.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed in Riyadh on September 29, the first high-level face-to-face meeting between the two Gulf states since their rift over Yemen, with Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman also attending as Houthi attacks on Saudi targets mounted.
UN special envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg held talks with Houthi negotiators in Muscat and with officials in Saudi Arabia as part of efforts to prevent further escalation of the fighting.

Yemen's Saudi-led coalition said early on September 26 it intercepted two ballistic missiles and two drones launched by the Houthis toward the kingdom, the missiles headed for Khamis Mushait and the drones for Riyadh. Saudi Arabia's military chiefs met in Riyadh with allies Pakistan and Turkey to review threats.

Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan arrived in Washington on September 28 for talks with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, as Riyadh seeks US help against the Houthis; Reuters sources said Washington agreed to intelligence and targeting support while declining to launch strikes itself.

Military chiefs from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey met in Riyadh under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement to review the threats facing the kingdom, condemning Houthi attacks and agreeing to deepen intelligence sharing and military coordination.
France confirmed on September 25 it will send troops, radars and air-defense systems to guard the oil terminal at Yanbu.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on September 21 that Britain would provide limited military support to Saudi Arabia, with the Royal Air Force (RAF) supplying defensive air-to-air refueling for Saudi aircraft on missions countering Houthi missile and drone attacks; the agreement runs for a matter of weeks and will be kept under review. The United States, which bombed the Houthis under the Biden and Trump administrations, has shown no interest in getting involved militarily this time.

A Houthi attack targeted Yanbu port, starting a fire inside the Red Sea port and prompting a temporary halt to loadings, according to maritime security firm Vanguard Tech. The strike came just days after Saudi Arabia repaired the East-West Pipeline following the September 10 drone hit and resumed crude loadings, with Kpler showing all seven crude berths at Yanbu and the Muajjiz terminal occupied on September 27.

No Iranian tankers loaded any crude in September, the first zero-lifting month in Kpler's tracking history back to 2013, analysts Yui Torikata and Nhway Khin Soe said. August loadings were 255,000 b/d across one VLCC, four suezmaxes, two aframaxes and one MR tanker, with the final lifting the 160,000-dwt suezmax Sarak from Kharg Island on August 25. Production was throttled to 2.06 million b/d, shore inventories sat at 66-70 million barrels (about 59% of capacity), and floating storage outside the blockade fell to 45 million barrels from 100 million in late July. Confirmed Iranian crude arrivals in China fell to about 468,000 b/d in September, roughly half June's level, though 'zombie' vessels with falsified AIS signals kept discharging obscured Iranian barrels at Chinese ports, peaking at 18 million barrels on nine VLCCs in August.

A Kuwait-flagged very large crude carrier, the 317,250-dwt Kazimah III operated by Kuwait Oil Tanker Company, was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on October 1, starting a fire aboard. UKMTO logged a third-party report without naming the vessel and said the crew was safe; maritime security firm Vanguard Tech identified the tanker. It was the second KOTC VLCC hit in four days, after the Al Funtas on September 28.

Flows through Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have climbed to almost 6 million barrels per day, close to June-July levels, with about 4.5 million b/d available for Red Sea exports, restoring Saudi Arabia's Hormuz bypass despite continued Houthi strikes.
